CORRECTED 2026-08-29. The authoring pass recorded here that the decomposition "matches the coefficients the book states"; that claim was FALSE for two of the four. An independent examiner found C and D swapped — printed C = 0, D = −2, correct C = −2, D = 0. Matching coefficients in 3v − v³ = A(v−1)(v²+1) + B(v+1)(v²+1) + (Cv+D)(v²−1) gives C = −2 from v³ and D = 0 from the constant term, and the identity fails for the printed pair at every v tested. The card contradicted itself one line later: the next step already integrates −2v/(v²+1), i.e. it used the correct values. The final relation y² − x² = c²(y² + x²)² was and is correct. insider_note: The denominator v³ − 3v factors as v(v² − 3), which does not match the numerator's factors — the book instead factors (v+1)(v−1)(v²+1) out of the RECIPROCAL of the whole fraction after cross-multiplying, so follow the book's exact rearrangement rather than trying to factor the original fraction directly.

steps.label: Recognise homogeneous form and substitute
steps.margin_note: One mark. Every term has total degree 3, so the equation is homogeneous.
steps.memory_tip: x³, xy², x²y and y³ are all degree 3 — homogeneous of degree 3.
lines: Take the dy term across and divide by dx:
Every term top and bottom has degree 3, so
steps.why: Moving the (3x²y − y³)dy term across the equals sign and dividing every term by x³ after substituting y = vx reduces the whole right side to a function of v alone, confirming the homogeneous form.
common_mistakes: Losing the sign when moving (3x²y − y³)dy to the other side of the equation.
Dividing the numerator and denominator by different powers of x.

steps.label: Separate the variables
steps.margin_note: One mark. Subtract v as a fraction with denominator (v³ − 3v).
steps.memory_tip: v(v³ − 3v) = v⁴ − 3v² is the term that cancels the −3v² inside the numerator.

lines.text: Take v to the right side:

steps.why: Writing v as v(v³ − 3v)/(v³ − 3v) puts both terms over the same denominator; expanding 1 − 3v² − v⁴ + 3v² leaves 1 − v⁴, giving a clean function of v.
common_mistakes: Losing the −v⁴ term when expanding v(v³ − 3v) = v⁴ − 3v².
Miscombining −3v² and +3v² and leaving a stray v² term behind.

steps.label: Write the partial fractions
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Factor 1 − v⁴ as (1−v)(1+v)(1+v²) and split the fraction into three pieces before integrating.
steps.memory_tip: 1 − v⁴ = (1 − v²)(1 + v²) = (1 − v)(1 + v)(1 + v²) — always factor a difference of squares twice.

lines.text: Coefficient of v³: −1 = A + B + C ⇒ C = −2

lines: and resolving into partial fractions gives A
steps.why: Splitting the single algebraic fraction into simpler pieces over each linear or quadratic factor is what lets each piece be integrated by a standard rule in the next step — this is the standard partial-fractions method for a rational function.
common_mistakes: Factoring 1 − v⁴ as (1 − v)²(1 + v)² instead of the correct (1−v)(1+v)(1+v²).
Forgetting the (Cv + D) numerator form required for the irreducible quadratic factor v² + 1.
lines_compact: and resolving into partial fractions gives A

steps.label: Integrate both sides
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Each of the three partial-fraction pieces integrates to a log.
steps.memory_tip: 1/(v+1) and 1/(v−1) both give logs; −2v/(v²+1) gives −log(v²+1), since 2v is the derivative of v² + 1.
steps.why: Each partial-fraction piece is a standard integral — 1/(v±1) gives a log, and 2v/(v²+1) gives a log of the quadratic — and combining the resulting logs with matching coefficients keeps the working compact before comparing with the right side.
common_mistakes: Treating 2v/(v²+1) as giving an inverse tangent instead of a log, since the numerator matches the derivative of the denominator.
Losing the factor of 1/2 in front of the two linear-factor logs.

steps.label: Final equation
steps.margin_note: The last mark. Square both sides to clear the square roots, then substitute v = y/x.
steps.memory_tip: Squaring removes both square roots at once: (√(v+1)√(v−1))² = (v+1)(v−1) = v² − 1.

lines.text: Equal logs have equal insides; square both
c² is an arbitrary constant; call it c:

steps.why: Squaring both sides of the earlier log-derived relation clears the square roots, and substituting v = y/x and multiplying both sides by x² turns the whole relation into a symmetric equation purely in x, y and the constant c.
common_mistakes: Squaring only one side of the equation instead of both.
Losing track of which power of x clears every v in the expression when substituting v = y/x.
